questions.modelAnswer: An async fn returns a Future, a value representing work that hasn't finished. Futures in Rust are lazy: nothing happens until something polls them, and the compiler turns each async fn into a state machine that can pause at every await. The standard library defines Future but no executor, so you add a runtime such as Tokio, which polls futures, parks them while they wait on I/O, and uses wakers to resume them when sockets or timers are ready. Awaiting a future runs it as part of the current task, one step after another; join! runs several futures concurrently within the task; tokio::spawn creates an independent task the runtime can run in parallel on its worker threads, which therefore requires the future to be Send and 'static. Async shines for many I/O-bound connections, such as web servers. Pitfalls: calling blocking code or heavy CPU work inside async code stalls the runtime's threads, so use spawn_blocking; and holding a std::sync::Mutex guard across an await can deadlock or make the future non-Send.

questions.title: unsafe Rust
questions.prompt: Explain what unsafe means in Rust. What extra operations does it allow, what guarantees do you take responsibility for, and how should unsafe code be wrapped in safe abstractions?

expectedConcepts.label: Raw pointer dereference, unsafe functions, FFI, mutable statics, unsafe traits
You uphold the invariants; the borrow checker still runs
Small unsafe blocks inside safe APIs, like Vec
Aliasing violations, data races; test with Miri

questions.modelAnswer: unsafe doesn't turn off the borrow checker; it unlocks a few extra operations: dereferencing raw pointers, calling unsafe functions including foreign C functions over FFI, accessing mutable statics, implementing unsafe traits like Send or Sync by hand, and accessing union fields. In return you promise to uphold the invariants the compiler can't check, such as pointers being valid and aligned, no aliasing &mut, and no data races; breaking them is undefined behaviour. The idiom is to keep unsafe blocks small, document why they are sound with a SAFETY comment, and wrap them in a safe API that cannot be misused from safe code. The standard library does exactly this: Vec, String and Mutex use unsafe internally but expose safe interfaces. Unsafe is also how Rust binds to C libraries. Risks: subtle aliasing and lifetime bugs; test unsafe code with Miri and keep it small enough to audit.

questions.title: String versus &str in Rust
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between String and &str in Rust. Cover ownership, how string slices work, UTF-8 and why you cannot index a string by position, and which type to use in function parameters.

expectedConcepts.label: String owns a growable heap buffer; &str borrows a slice
Always valid UTF-8; chars vs bytes
Take &str in parameters; deref coercion from &String
No indexing by position; slicing mid-character panics

questions.modelAnswer: String is an owned, growable, heap-allocated buffer of text: you can push to it and it is freed when its owner goes out of scope. &str is a borrowed string slice, a pointer and a length pointing into text owned by something else: a String, or the program binary for string literals, which have type &'static str. Both are always valid UTF-8, so one character can take one to four bytes. That's why Rust doesn't let you index s[3]: a position in bytes might be the middle of a character, and a position in characters would be O(n). Use .chars() for Unicode scalar values and .bytes() for raw bytes, and byte-range slicing like &s[0..4] panics if it doesn't fall on a character boundary. For function parameters, take &str: it accepts string literals and, through deref coercion, &String, without forcing callers to allocate. Return String when you create new text, and convert with to_string or to_owned.

questions.title: Copy, Clone and Drop in Rust
questions.prompt: Explain the Copy, Clone and Drop traits in Rust. Which types are Copy, why can't a type be both Copy and Drop, and when does a value get dropped?

expectedConcepts.label: Copy is an implicit bitwise copy; Clone is an explicit, possibly deep copy
Drop runs cleanup when a value goes out of scope
Integers, bools, chars, shared references are Copy; String and Vec are not
Copy and Drop are mutually exclusive; mem::forget; clone costs

questions.modelAnswer: By default, assigning or passing a value moves it. If a type implements Copy, the value is instead copied implicitly with a simple bitwise copy, and the original stays usable. Integers, floats, bool, char, shared references and tuples or arrays of Copy types are Copy; String, Vec and Box are not, because copying their bits would create two owners of the same heap buffer. Clone is an explicit .clone() that can do a deep copy, like duplicating a String's buffer, so its cost is visible in the code; you can derive both. Drop is Rust's destructor: its drop method runs automatically when a value goes out of scope, in reverse order of declaration, which is how RAII frees memory, closes files and releases locks. A type can't be both Copy and Drop, because implicit copies would make it unclear how many times cleanup runs. You can drop early with drop(x); std::mem::forget skips the destructor. Pitfall: cloning large values in hot loops just to satisfy the borrow checker.

questions.title: The JVM, JIT and garbage collection
questions.prompt: Explain how Java code runs on the JVM and how garbage collection works. Cover bytecode and JIT compilation, the heap and generational collection, and what causes GC pauses.

expectedConcepts.label: javac compiles to bytecode run by the JVM
JIT; reachability from GC roots; young and old generations
Stop-the-world pauses, G1/ZGC, heap sizing
Leaks via unintended references; OutOfMemoryError

questions.modelAnswer: javac compiles Java into platform-independent bytecode. The JVM loads classes, interprets the bytecode at first, profiles it, and JIT-compiles hot methods into optimised machine code. Objects live on the heap, and the garbage collector frees objects that are no longer reachable from GC roots such as thread stacks and static fields. Most objects die young, so collectors are generational: frequent, cheap collections of the young generation and rarer collections of the old generation. Modern collectors such as G1 (the default) and ZGC do much of their work concurrently to keep pauses short, but stop-the-world pauses still happen and grow with live data and allocation rate. Java can still leak memory: objects kept reachable by mistake, for example in static maps, caches or listeners that are never removed, until an OutOfMemoryError.

questions.title: equals, hashCode and HashMap in Java
questions.prompt: Explain the contract between equals and hashCode in Java, how HashMap uses them, and what goes wrong if you override one without the other or use mutable fields in a key.

expectedConcepts.label: Equal objects must have equal hash codes
hashCode picks the bucket, equals finds the key
Objects.hash / Objects.equals, records
Missed lookups, duplicates, mutable keys

questions.modelAnswer: The contract: if a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode(). The reverse need not hold, because collisions are allowed. HashMap and HashSet use hashCode to choose a bucket, then equals to find the matching key inside it. If you override equals but not hashCode, two equal keys usually land in different buckets, so lookups miss and a set can hold "duplicates". If a key's fields change after it is inserted, its hash changes and the entry becomes unreachable. Base both methods on the same immutable fields, use Objects.hash and Objects.equals, or use records, which generate both correctly.

questions.title: Visibility, volatile and executors in Java
questions.prompt: Explain the basics of the Java memory model: visibility, the volatile keyword, synchronized and happens-before. When would you use an ExecutorService or virtual threads instead of creating threads by hand?

expectedConcepts.label: Writes may be invisible or reordered without happens-before
volatile, synchronized, atomics
Thread pools, futures, virtual threads
volatile is not atomic; check-then-act; deadlocks

questions.modelAnswer: Without synchronisation, one thread's writes may never become visible to another, and operations can be reordered. The Java memory model defines happens-before rules: unlocking a monitor happens-before every later lock of the same monitor, and a write to a volatile field happens-before later reads of that field. volatile gives visibility and ordering, but not atomicity: count++ on a volatile int is still a race, so use AtomicInteger or a lock. synchronized gives mutual exclusion plus visibility. Rather than creating threads by hand, submit tasks to an ExecutorService, which manages a thread pool, returns futures and shuts down cleanly. Since Java 21, virtual threads make one thread per task cheap for blocking I/O. Pitfalls: check-then-act races and deadlocks from inconsistent lock ordering.

questions.title: Java collections: ArrayList, LinkedList and HashMap
questions.prompt: Compare ArrayList and LinkedList in Java, and explain how HashMap works internally, including buckets, resizing and treeification. What are the time complexities, and when would you choose each collection?

expectedConcepts.label: ArrayList is a resizable array; LinkedList is doubly linked
Buckets, load factor 0.75, resize, tree bins
ArrayList by default; ArrayDeque for queues; LinkedHashMap/TreeMap
ConcurrentModificationException; HashMap not thread-safe

questions.modelAnswer: ArrayList is a resizable array: get(i) is O(1), adding at the end is amortised O(1), and inserting or removing in the middle is O(n) because elements shift. LinkedList is a doubly linked list: adding or removing at the ends is O(1), but get(i) is O(n), and every node is a separate object, so it uses more memory and has poor cache locality. In practice ArrayList is the default, and ArrayDeque is better than LinkedList for queues and stacks. HashMap is an array of buckets: it hashes the key, picks a bucket, and stores entries there; equals finds the right key within a bucket. When the size exceeds capacity times the load factor (0.75 by default), it doubles the array and redistributes entries. Since Java 8, a bucket with many collisions turns into a red-black tree, so the worst case is O(log n) instead of O(n). Use LinkedHashMap for insertion order or LRU caches and TreeMap for sorted keys. Pitfalls: modifying a collection while iterating throws ConcurrentModificationException (use the iterator's remove), and HashMap is not thread-safe; use ConcurrentHashMap.

questions.title: Generics and type erasure in Java
questions.prompt: Explain generics in Java and type erasure. What can't you do because types are erased at runtime, and what do bounded wildcards like extends and super mean?

expectedConcepts.label: Type parameters are checked at compile time, then erased
? extends, ? super, PECS
Type-safe collections without casts; generic methods
No new T(), no instanceof List<String>, no primitives

questions.modelAnswer: Generics let classes and methods take type parameters, like List<String>, so the compiler checks types and inserts casts for you, giving type-safe collections without manual casting. Java implements them with type erasure: after checking, the compiler replaces type parameters with their bounds, usually Object, so at runtime List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class. That's why you can't write new T(), check instanceof List<String>, create a generic array, or use primitives like List<int>; you pass a Class<T> token when you need the type at runtime. Wildcards express variance: List<? extends Number> can be read as Numbers but you can't add to it, while List<? super Integer> accepts Integers but reads as Object. The rule of thumb is PECS: producer extends, consumer super, as in Collections.copy. Pitfalls: raw types and unchecked casts bypass the checks and cause ClassCastException later.

questions.title: Checked and unchecked exceptions in Java
questions.prompt: Explain Java's exception hierarchy and the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions. Cover try-with-resources, and the best practices for throwing and catching exceptions.

expectedConcepts.label: Throwable: Error and Exception; RuntimeException
Checked must be declared or caught; unchecked need not
try-with-resources closes AutoCloseable
Don't swallow; keep the cause; avoid catching Exception broadly

questions.modelAnswer: Everything thrown in Java is a Throwable, which splits into Error, for serious JVM problems like OutOfMemoryError that you normally don't catch, and Exception. Checked exceptions, such as IOException, must be either caught or declared in the method's throws clause, so the compiler forces callers to think about them. Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException, such as NullPointerException or IllegalArgumentException, and usually signal programming errors; they don't need declaring. try-with-resources, try (var in = Files.newInputStream(path)) { ... }, closes any AutoCloseable automatically, even on exceptions, replacing error-prone finally blocks. Best practices: catch only what you can handle, at the right level; wrap low-level exceptions in meaningful ones while keeping the original as the cause; never leave an empty catch block; don't use exceptions for normal control flow; and avoid catching Exception or Throwable broadly, which hides bugs.

questions.title: Interfaces versus abstract classes in Java
questions.prompt: Compare interfaces and abstract classes in Java. Cover default methods, multiple inheritance of type, state, and how sealed interfaces and records are used in modern Java.

expectedConcepts.label: Class can implement many interfaces but extend one class; abstract classes hold state
Default methods, sealed, records
Interfaces for contracts; abstract classes for shared implementation
Diamond conflicts with defaults; fragile base classes

questions.modelAnswer: An interface defines a contract: methods a class promises to provide. A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class. An abstract class can hold state (fields), constructors and partly implemented methods, so it suits a family of closely related classes sharing code, as in the template method pattern. Since Java 8, interfaces can have default and static methods, which lets libraries add methods without breaking implementers, but interfaces still can't hold instance state. Modern Java adds records, concise immutable data carriers with generated constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString, and sealed interfaces, which list exactly which classes may implement them; together with pattern matching in switch, the compiler can check that every case is handled. Prefer interfaces plus composition for flexibility. Pitfalls: two interfaces providing the same default method force you to override it to resolve the conflict, and deep abstract-class hierarchies become fragile when a base class changes.

questions.title: Streams and lambdas in Java
questions.prompt: Explain lambdas and the Stream API in Java. Cover functional interfaces, intermediate versus terminal operations, laziness, collectors, and when parallel streams or plain loops are a better choice.

expectedConcepts.label: Lambdas implement functional interfaces
Intermediate (lazy) vs terminal operations; collectors
Declarative pipelines; loops for simple or performance-critical code
Side effects, reusing streams, misused parallel streams

questions.modelAnswer: A lambda like x -> x * 2 is a short implementation of a functional interface, an interface with a single abstract method such as Function, Predicate, Supplier or Runnable; method references like String::length are shorthand for lambdas. The Stream API processes collections declaratively: list.stream().filter(...).map(...).collect(Collectors.toList()). Intermediate operations like filter, map and sorted are lazy and return a new stream; nothing runs until a terminal operation such as collect, forEach, count or reduce, which lets the pipeline stop early with findFirst. Collectors like groupingBy and joining build maps and strings. Streams are readable for transformations, but plain loops are fine, and sometimes faster, for simple or performance-critical code; use IntStream to avoid boxing. Pitfalls: side effects inside lambdas, reusing a stream after a terminal operation (IllegalStateException), and parallel streams, which share the common ForkJoinPool and only help for large, CPU-bound, independent work.

questions.title: The JavaScript event loop
questions.prompt: Explain the JavaScript event loop. Cover the call stack, the task queue and the microtask queue, and why a Promise callback runs before a setTimeout callback scheduled with zero delay.

expectedConcepts.label: One thread and call stack; async work handled by the runtime
Task (macrotask) queue vs microtask queue
Microtasks drain after each task, so promises run before timeouts
Long synchronous work blocks the loop; use workers

questions.modelAnswer: JavaScript runs your code on a single thread with one call stack. Slow operations such as timers, network requests and file I/O are handled by the browser or Node, which queue a callback when they finish. The event loop runs one task (macrotask) at a time, such as a setTimeout callback or an event handler, and after each task it drains the whole microtask queue: Promise reactions, queueMicrotask callbacks and code after an await. That's why Promise.resolve().then(a) runs before setTimeout(b, 0): a is a microtask processed as soon as the current script finishes, while b waits for a later task. Pitfalls: long synchronous work blocks the loop, freezing the UI or stalling a server, and endless microtask chains can starve rendering. Move CPU-heavy work to Web Workers or worker threads.

questions.title: Closures and this in JavaScript
questions.prompt: Explain closures in JavaScript and how the value of this is determined. Give an example of a closure, and explain how arrow functions differ from regular functions.

expectedConcepts.label: A function keeps access to variables of the scope where it was created
this depends on the call site; arrow functions use lexical this
Private state, counters, callbacks, event handlers
Losing this in callbacks; var in loops; retained memory

questions.modelAnswer: A closure is a function together with the variables from the scope where it was created; it can keep using them after the outer function has returned. Example: function counter() { let n = 0; return () => ++n; }. Each counter has its own private n. Closures power callbacks, event handlers, module privacy and memoisation. For regular functions, this is decided at the call site: obj.method() sets this to obj, a plain call gives undefined in strict mode, new sets it to the new object, and call, apply and bind set it explicitly. Arrow functions have no this of their own; they use the this of the enclosing scope, which makes them handy as callbacks inside methods. Pitfalls: losing this when passing obj.method as a callback, var in loops sharing one variable (use let), and closures keeping large objects alive.

questions.title: TypeScript's type system
questions.prompt: Explain TypeScript's type system. Cover structural typing, type inference, union types with narrowing, and why types are erased at runtime, including what that means for validating API data.

expectedConcepts.label: Static, structural typing checked at compile time
Inference, unions, narrowing, type guards, generics
Validate untrusted data at runtime, e.g. with Zod
Types are erased; any and as assertions hide bugs

questions.modelAnswer: TypeScript adds static types that are checked at compile time and then erased: the output is plain JavaScript. Typing is structural, so a value fits a type if it has the required shape, whatever its declared name. The compiler infers most types from initial values and return statements. Union types, such as string | number or discriminated unions like { kind: 'ok' } | { kind: 'error' }, are narrowed with typeof, in, checks on the discriminant, or custom type guards. Because types vanish at runtime, data from fetch or JSON.parse is untrusted: type it as unknown and validate it with a schema library such as Zod before using it. Pitfalls: any and as assertions silence the checker and let wrong data through.

questions.title: Prototypes and classes in JavaScript
questions.prompt: Explain prototypal inheritance in JavaScript. How does property lookup follow the prototype chain, and how do ES6 classes relate to prototypes?

expectedConcepts.label: Lookup walks the prototype chain until found or null
__proto__ / Object.getPrototypeOf, constructor .prototype, class, extends
Methods shared via the prototype save memory
Mutating built-in prototypes; class fields vs methods; this binding

questions.modelAnswer: Every JavaScript object has an internal link to another object, its prototype. When you read a property, the engine looks on the object itself, then on its prototype, then that object's prototype, up the prototype chain until it finds the property or reaches null; Object.prototype sits near the top, which is why every object has toString. Object.create(proto) makes an object with a chosen prototype, and Object.getPrototypeOf reads it. A constructor function's .prototype object becomes the prototype of instances created with new, so methods placed there are shared by all instances: one copy in memory. ES6 classes are mostly syntactic sugar over this: class methods go on the prototype, extends links the prototypes, and super calls the parent's version. Pitfalls: modifying built-in prototypes like Array.prototype breaks other code, arrow-function class fields create a separate function per instance rather than one shared method, and for...in also iterates inherited enumerable properties, so check hasOwnProperty or use Object.keys.

questions.title: Promises and async/await in JavaScript
questions.prompt: Explain promises and async/await in JavaScript. Cover promise states, chaining, error handling, and the difference between Promise.all, Promise.allSettled and Promise.race.

expectedConcepts.label: Pending, fulfilled, rejected; settles once
then/catch chaining; async functions return promises; await
all fails fast; allSettled waits for all; race takes the first
Unhandled rejections; sequential awaits in loops; forgotten await

questions.modelAnswer: A promise represents a value that will be available later. It starts pending and settles once, either fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error. then registers what to do with the value and returns a new promise, so steps chain; catch handles a rejection anywhere earlier in the chain. An async function always returns a promise, and await pauses that function until a promise settles, letting you write sequential-looking code with try/catch for errors. To run work concurrently, start the promises first and combine them: Promise.all waits for all and rejects as soon as any one fails, Promise.allSettled waits for every result and reports each outcome, and Promise.race settles with whichever finishes first, which is useful for timeouts; Promise.any takes the first success. Pitfalls: forgetting await, unhandled rejections that crash Node or are silently lost, awaiting inside a loop when the calls could run in parallel, and using async callbacks with forEach, which doesn't wait for them.

questions.title: var, let, const, hoisting and equality
questions.prompt: Explain the differences between var, let and const in JavaScript, including hoisting and the temporal dead zone. Then explain type coercion and why === is usually preferred over ==.

expectedConcepts.label: var is function-scoped; let and const are block-scoped
Hoisting and the temporal dead zone
== coerces types; === compares without coercion
const objects are still mutable; NaN; surprising coercions

questions.modelAnswer: var is function-scoped and can be redeclared; let and const are block-scoped, so a variable declared inside an if or a loop stays there. const prevents reassigning the variable, but the object it points to can still be mutated unless you freeze it. All declarations are hoisted to the top of their scope, but differently: a var is initialised to undefined, so reading it early gives undefined, while let and const sit in the temporal dead zone until their line runs, so reading them early throws a ReferenceError. That makes bugs easier to spot. == compares after type coercion, with surprising results like 0 == '' and '1' == 1 being true, while === compares value and type without coercion, so it is predictable and preferred; a common exception is x == null, which checks for both null and undefined. Also, NaN is not equal to itself; use Number.isNaN. Default to const, use let when you must reassign, and avoid var.

questions.title: ES modules versus CommonJS
questions.prompt: Explain JavaScript modules. Compare ES modules with CommonJS, covering import and export, static versus dynamic loading, tree shaking, and how Node.js decides which format a file uses.

expectedConcepts.label: ESM import/export vs CommonJS require/module.exports
ESM is static and async; CommonJS is dynamic and synchronous
Static structure enables tree shaking and code splitting
package.json type, .mjs/.cjs; interop headaches

questions.modelAnswer: CommonJS is Node's original module system: require() loads a module synchronously and returns its module.exports object, and because require is just a function call it can happen anywhere, even conditionally. ES modules are the standard: import and export declarations at the top level, so the dependency graph is known statically before the code runs; loading is asynchronous, imports are live bindings, top-level await is allowed, and import() loads a module dynamically when needed. Because the structure is static, bundlers like Vite, Rollup or webpack can tree-shake unused exports and split code into chunks. In Node, a .mjs file is always ESM and a .cjs file always CommonJS; for .js files, the nearest package.json's "type": "module" makes them ESM, otherwise CommonJS. Pitfalls: mixing the two is awkward, older Node versions can't require ESM, and __dirname doesn't exist in ESM, so you use import.meta.url instead.

questions.title: Generics and utility types in TypeScript
questions.prompt: Explain generics in TypeScript and common utility types such as Partial, Pick, Omit and Record. How do keyof and mapped types work, and when do advanced types become a problem?

expectedConcepts.label: Type parameters preserve the relationship between inputs and outputs
Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, keyof, mapped types
Derive types from one source of truth; constraints with extends
Unreadable types, slow compiles, any leaking

questions.modelAnswer: Generics let a function or type work with many types while keeping the relationship between them: function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined returns the same type the array holds, unlike returning any. Constraints narrow what T can be, as in <T extends { id: string }>. keyof T is the union of T's property names, and a mapped type like { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] } builds a new type by transforming each property; that is exactly how Partial<T> works. Built-in utility types cover common needs: Partial<T> makes all fields optional (good for update payloads), Required<T> the opposite, Pick<T, 'a' | 'b'> and Omit<T, 'password'> select fields, Record<K, V> types dictionaries, and ReturnType extracts a function's result type. They let you derive types from one source of truth instead of copying them. Pitfalls: deeply nested conditional and mapped types become unreadable, produce confusing error messages and slow the compiler; prefer simple, explicit types where possible.
